items.content: The rain arrived after midnight, tapping at first against the nylon shell like a hesitant visitor, then settling into a full and steady roar that swallowed every other sound. Inside, zipped into the warm dark, you felt both impossibly small and perfectly contained — a seed in a pod, a letter in an envelope. The world had been reduced to this: the drum of water inches above your face, the smell of wet earth rising through the seams, and the strange, sourceless comfort of being sheltered by something so thin.

items.content: The dust moves slowly here, caught in slanted light that falls between the shelves like something forgotten. A woman turns a page near the window, and the sound of it travels the whole room. Somewhere deeper in the stacks, a cart rolls a few inches and stops, as if reconsidering. This is the hour the library keeps for itself — unhurried, unwitnessed — when the books seem less like objects and more like presences, breathing quietly in their long rows.

items.content: The last day stretched out golden and reluctant, the way summer always did at its end — longer in feeling than in hours. We rode our bikes until the streetlights flickered on, pretending not to notice the school clothes laid out on our beds at home, stiff and accusatory. The air smelled faintly of cut grass and something else, something harder to name, like the season itself was already becoming a memory. By nightfall, we were quieter than usual, understanding without words that childhood moved in only one direction.

items.content: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity.
